item.title: Go Daily Question 155
item.description:
What is the output of the following code?

    "fmt"
)

    ShowA() int
}

}

    return w.i + 10
}

}

    c := Work{3}

}

item.title: Go Daily Question 144
item.description:
What is the output of the following code?

type People struct{}

func (p *People) ShowA() {
    fmt.Println("showA")
    p.ShowB()
}
func (p *People) ShowB() {
    fmt.Println("showB")
}

type Teacher struct {
    People
}

func (t *Teacher) ShowB() {
    fmt.Println("teacher showB")
}

func main() {
    t := Teacher{}
    t.ShowB()
}
🔑 Answer Analysis: 
teacher showB

Run online

Key Takeaway: Struct Embedding

The Teacher struct embeds the People struct. In an embedded struct, People is called the inner type, and Teacher is called the outer type; through embedding, the inner type’s attributes and methods become available to the outer type, as if they were its own. Additionally, the outer type can define its own attributes and methods, and even define methods with the same name as those in the inner type, in which case the inner type’s methods will be “shadowed”. ShowB() in this example is such a method with the same name.

item.title: Go Daily Question 110
item.description:
If the calling code for the Add() function is:

func main() {
    var a Integer = 1
    var b Integer = 2
    var i interface{} = &a
    sum := i.(*Integer).Add(b)
    fmt.Println(sum)
}

Then the correct definition for the Add function is:

A.
type Integer int
func (a Integer) Add(b Integer) Integer {
        return a + b
}

B.
type Integer int
func (a Integer) Add(b *Integer) Integer {
        return a + *b
}

C.
type Integer int
func (a *Integer) Add(b Integer) Integer {
        return *a + b
}

D.
type Integer int
func (a *Integer) Add(b *Integer) Integer {
        return *a + *b
}
🔑 Answer Analysis:

AC If it’s func (a Integer), the compiler will automatically add func (a *Integer) for you. The reverse is not true.

item.title: Go Daily Question 056
item.description:
What is the output of the following code?

type People struct{}

func (p *People) ShowA() {
    fmt.Println("showA")
    p.ShowB()
}
func (p *People) ShowB() {
    fmt.Println("showB")
}

type Teacher struct {
    People
}

func (t *Teacher) ShowB() {
    fmt.Println("teacher showB")
}

func main() {
    t := Teacher{}
    t.ShowA()
}
🔑 Answer Analysis:

Answer: “showA” “showB”

t.ShowA() will prioritize calling its own ShowA(). However, since it’s not defined in the problem, it calls the parent struct’s ShowA(). When it reaches p.ShowB(), note that p is *People, the parent struct, and it will call p’s own ShowB(). Therefore, the output is: “showA” “showB”

item.title: Go Daily Question 052
item.description:
What is the output of the following code?

type People struct{}

func (p *People) ShowA() {
    fmt.Println("showA")
    p.ShowB()
}
func (p *People) ShowB() {
    fmt.Println("showB")
}

type Teacher struct {
    People
}

func (t *Teacher) ShowB() {
    fmt.Println("teacher showB")
}

func main() {
    t := Teacher{}
    t.ShowB()
}
🔑 Answer Analysis:

Answer: teacher showB t.ShowB() will use its own existing ShowB(). If you want to use the parent struct’s (People) ShowB(), you need to change it to t.People.ShowB().
